title: The Seconds That Grew After the Fall — Stetson & Eagleman's 31-Meter Free-Fall Flicker Experiment, Oddball Predictability & Duration vs. Passage-of-Time Judgments

teenKit.tldr: When facing life-threatening danger, your brain doesn't actually process the world in slow motion; instead, terrifying memories just feel stretched out when you look back at them later. Time doesn't speed up or slow down objectively—our brains are just expert tricksters when it comes to editing our memories.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how our brains warp time helps us realize that our memories of high-stress events, trauma, and everyday moments are deeply subjective reconstructions rather than exact video recordings.
keyTakeaways: In a 31-meter free-fall experiment, people retrospectively judged their fall as lasting 36% longer than it actually was, but their real-time visual processing speed (tested via wrist-LED flicker) didn't actually change at all.
The brain handles unexpected surprises ("oddballs") differently than routine events, making rare stimuli feel like they take up more time because they require more neural processing power.

Psychological research shows a distinct difference between how long we think an event lasted (duration estimation) and how fast we feel time is currently dragging or flying by (passage-of-time judgments).

vocab.meaning: The branch of science that quantitatively investigates the relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations and perceptions they affect.
Evaluating how long an event lasted only after it has already happened, relying heavily on memory rather than a live mental stopwatch.
The psychological phenomenon where a surprising or unexpected stimulus in a sequence of normal events feels like it takes longer to happen.
The brain's illusion that time is stretching out, making seconds feel like they are lasting much longer than they physically are.

quiz.question: According to Stetson and Eagleman's free-fall study, what actually happens to our visual processing speed when we are terrified?
options: It speeds up dramatically like a high-speed camera
It remains completely unchanged while memory creates the illusion of slow motion
It shuts down entirely to protect the brain from trauma
It slows down so we can process more details per second
quiz.explanation: The wrist-LED flicker test proved that real-time visual resolution doesn't improve during a fall; the feeling of slow motion is a trick of memory after the fact.

quiz.question: Why do unexpected events or 'oddballs' tend to feel like they take up more time?
options: Because novelty requires more neural processing power and detail encoding
Because clocks physically tick slower when you are surprised
Because adrenaline physically alters the speed of light hitting your retinas
Because you stop breathing temporarily during a shock
quiz.explanation: When something unexpected happens, your brain packs more data into its memory banks, which makes the event feel longer when you look back at it.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between duration estimates and passage-of-time judgments?
options: One is used exclusively by scientists and the other by artists
Duration estimates measure how long an event lasted, while passage-of-time judgments measure how fast time feels like it is moving right now
Duration estimates only apply to the past, while passage-of-time applies only to the future
There is no real difference; scientists use the terms interchangeably
quiz.explanation: Research shows a clear psychological separation between calculating how much time has passed versus how fast or slow the current moment feels like it's dragging.
